instagram.caption:
2.3 million people answered a poll. It still picked the wrong president.

In 1936 the Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots and got about 2.3 million back. It predicted Alf Landon would win with 57%. Franklin Roosevelt won 60.8% and 46 of 48 states.

Two things went wrong:
1. The list. Names came from car registrations, phone books and magazine subscribers. During the Depression those people were richer than average.
2. Who replied. Only about 1 in 4 answered, and the people unhappy with Roosevelt were keener to send the card back.

The lesson for every survey, poll and feedback form: a bigger sample shrinks random error, but it does nothing about who is missing.

Try the free lab on kaizen-desk-mba.pages.dev (link in bio). Survey 10,000 invented employees four ways and see which one finds the truth.

Sources: Literary Digest poll data, randomservices.org. Lusinchi, Social Science History, 2012.

In 1936 the Literary Digest ran the biggest poll in history. About 10 million ballots went out and 2.3 million came back. It predicted Alf Landon would win with 57%.

Roosevelt won 60.8% and 46 of 48 states.

The list came from car registrations, phone books and magazine subscribers, which skewed rich during the Depression. And only about 1 in 4 replied, mostly people with strong views.

I see the same pattern in employee pulse surveys and customer feedback today. A big response count feels safe. It is not. Size shrinks random error. It does nothing about who is missing.
